proposed_edges.relationship: A call to study ‘the history of both women and men’ and ‘the significance of the sexes, of gender groups’, quoted by Joan Scott as an early relational use of gender (1975–76; Scott 1986)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: A reader’s explicit claim, read. Scott, ‘Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis’, AHR 91:5 (1986), p. 1054: those who wanted ‘a relational notion’ used ‘gender’; ‘Thus Natalie Davis suggested in 1975, “It seems to me that we should be interested in the history of both women and men, that we should not be working only on the subjected sex any more than an historian of class can focus entirely on peasants. Our goal is to understand the significance of the sexes, of gender groups in the historical past.”’ (n. 4, citing Feminist Studies 3, Winter 1975–76, p. 90). Davis’s 1976 article is unread; her words are as Scott quotes them. Her own retrospect (1997, p. 16, read) describes the same programme: ‘examining the range of relations between and concepts about women and men in different times and places’. The Holberg committee (2010, read): ‘Her work brings gender to the fore’. A precursor statement taken up in Scott’s argument, not a claim that Davis founded gender history or shared Scott’s later theoretical position.

proposed_edges.relationship: Women and the relations of the sexes in early modern towns and festive life, and, with Jill Conway, a first Canadian course in women’s history (1971–75)
proposed_edges.map_label: Society and the Sexes; city women, 1971–75
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own retrospect (Haskins Lecture, 1997, read in full): ‘In 1971, Jill and I organized the first course in women’s history in Canada, Society and the Sexes in Early Modern Europe and in America’ (p. 16, her claim); ‘City Women and Religious Change’ and ‘Women on Top’ show ‘this hope to build upon rather than abandon one form of history for another’ (p. 15); the field meant ‘simultaneously writing women into the historical record’, ‘examining the range of relations between and concepts about women and men’ and ‘re-evaluating the meaning of movements like the Reformation’ (p. 16). Hesse (AHA memorial, 2024, read in excerpts): ‘Her most transformative course was Society and the Sexes, a first in introducing the history of women’ into university curricula. Nussdorfer (SCS memorial, read) records two Sixteenth Century Society prizes in her name in early modern women’s, gender and sexuality studies. The 1970s essays (in Society and Culture, 1975) are unread; their content is as she describes it. edge_071 separately records the course as a route into Women on the Margins.

proposed_edges.relationship: Festive misrule and religious riot read as culturally patterned action, with violence ‘related here less to the pathological than to the normal’ (1971–75)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own text. ‘The Rites of Violence’ (Past & Present 59, 1973; pp. 52–53, 57, 60–61 and 90–91 read): violence is explained ‘in terms of the goals of their actions and in terms of the rôles and patterns of behaviour allowed by their culture. Religious violence is related here less to the pathological than to the normal’; it had ‘a connection in time, place and form with the life of worship’ (p. 90); crowd violence has ‘some structure to it — here dramatic and ritual’ (p. 91). She sets this against Estèbe’s appeal to the ‘collective unconscious’ (p. 90). Her retrospect (1997, read): ‘The Reasons of Misrule’ began in 1969 from Van Gennep and Bakhtin (pp. 13–14); the title Society and Culture (1975) ‘seemed quite fresh and anthropological at the time’ (p. 15). Reception: Hunt’s New Cultural History (1989) makes ‘Thompson and Davis’ one of its models for cultural history in Desan’s chapter (publisher contents; chapter unread), and the graph’s earlier reading of Hunt’s introduction records her among its formative resources. Holberg committee (2010); Hesse (2024): ‘methodologically heterodox, incorporating anthropological and literary approaches’. Estèbe’s 1975 comment on ‘Rites’ and Davis’s rejoinder (Past & Present 67) are unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Lyon’s printing workers, a journeymen’s organization and the religious crowd: urban social history that keeps conflict, interest and several social axes (1959–75)
proposed_edges.map_label: Lyon’s menu peuple and the crowd, 1959–75
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own texts. ‘The Rites of Violence’ (1973, p. 53, read) builds on the crowd history ‘of George Rudé, Eric Hobsbawm, E. P. Thompson, Charles Tilly, Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie and others’ and extends it to religious riot, which ‘has not received analytical attention’. Retrospect (1997, read): her 1959 dissertation found Lyon’s Protestants ‘drawn from all the social orders’, organized ‘around the axis of emotional-spiritual class’, and she prefers ‘the concept of multiple axes … as contrasted with my earlier two-dimensional Marxist model’ (p. 11); ‘A Trade Union in Sixteenth-Century France’ (1966) was ‘my commitment to classic social history’ (p. 12), with unease at the ‘evolutionary approach’ of Hobsbawm’s Primitive Rebels (p. 13); ‘Conflict was part of the picture, not just community’ (p. 15). Nussdorfer (SCS memorial, read): ‘the rare social historian who valued printed sources’. The 1966 article is unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Thompson’s moral economy of the crowd, acknowledged and applied to the legitimation of religious riot (1973)
proposed_edges.map_label: Moral economy into the religious crowd, 1973
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her acknowledgement, in period. ‘The Rites of Violence’ (1973, read): n. 6 on p. 53 lists ‘those works which have especially assisted the preparation of this paper’, including Thompson, ‘The Moral Economy of the English Crowd in the Eighteenth Century’ (Past and Present, 1971). On p. 61: ‘E. P. Thompson has shown how in the eighteenth-century English food-riot, the crowd’s behaviour was legitimated by a widely held belief that it was acting in place of the government … Now we can deduce some of the same assumptions from the actions of the religious crowds of the mid-sixteenth century’ (n. 26, citing pp. 91–115). Rudé, Hobsbawm, Tilly and Le Roy Ladurie are named as well; Thompson is one resource among several. Their correspondence of 1970–72 is edited by Walsham (2017; opening extract only).

proposed_edges.relationship: Her study of French youth abbeys and charivaris used by Thompson as ‘une étude importante’ in his essay on English rough music (1971–72)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Thompson’s own text, read in excerpts. ‘« Rough Music » : le charivari anglais’, Annales ESC 27 (1972), in the 2020 Socio-anthropologie reprint (paragraph numbers; no Annales pages): ‘Dans une étude importante, Natalie Davis a examiné certains aspects du charivari en France au xvie siècle’ (¶36); he uses her findings on the kinds of charivari and the ‘quasi-institutionalised’ role of youth abbeys, citing ‘The Reasons of Misrule’ (Past and Present 50, 1971, pp. 41–75; n. 40), with further uses at nn. 51 and 59. He reads her as following Lévi-Strauss on ‘la masse de jeunes disponibles’ (¶48), which is his characterisation. Walsham (2017; opening extract read) calls the two essays ‘classics of twentieth-century historical writing’ and edits their letters of 1970–72 (unread). Hunt’s volume (1989) pairs them as a model for cultural history (Desan; chapter unread).

proposed_edges.relationship: Van Gennep’s folklore and Douglas on pollution and boundaries, then Evans-Pritchard, Turner, Geertz and Mintz, read for questions tested on sixteenth-century evidence (1969–1980s)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her acknowledgements, in period and in retrospect. 1973 (read): ‘For the theory in this paragraph, I have found helpful Mary Douglas’s remarks on the relation between pollution fears and concern for social boundaries (Purity and Danger … ch. 7)’ (p. 61, n. 25); Van Gennep’s Manuel de folklore français on the dead (p. 57, n. 17). 1997 (read in full): she found Van Gennep’s Manuel, but her essay ‘used only historical evidence’ and, ‘in contrast with the static unchanging portrait of ceremonial and customary life presented in Van Gennep’, ‘pointed to shifts’ (p. 14); ‘I went on to read in anthropology and folklore: E.E. Evans-Pritchard, Victor Turner, Clifford Geertz, Sidney Mintz, and many others … I read eclectically, indifferent to conflicts within anthropology, for I was not looking for solutions, but for questions’ (p. 14); ‘One term I co-taught a course with Clifford Geertz’ (p. 19); the Martin Guerre project ‘grew out of the practice of anthropological history’ (p. 17). Finlay (1988, p. 554, read) attributes the book’s ‘inventive aspects’ to ‘anthropology, ethnography, and literary criticism’. No single anthropologist is credited as the source, and no specifically Geertzian method is established.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Return of Martin Guerre: a village imposture reconstructed from legal, notarial and printed sources as conjectural ‘ethnography’, reached ‘via film’ (1982–83)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own account (1997, p. 19, read): ‘Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie and Carlo Ginzburg came to write their splendid microhistories … as an expansion of their prose. I came to microhistory (or what I called ethnography) via film’; making a film ‘could be an approximation of the ethnographic experience’ (p. 18). Her method (‘On the Lame’, 1988, pp. 574–575, read): Coras, Le Sueur and the Parlement registers, set in ‘concentric circles of research’ through village and criminal archives; ‘I worked as a detective … establishing a conjectural argument that made the best sense, the most plausible sense, of sixteenth-century evidence’, citing Collingwood and Ginzburg’s ‘Clues’ (History Workshop 9, 1980; n. 11). Reception: Finlay (1988, p. 553, read) places the book with Le Roy Ladurie’s and Ginzburg’s legal-record reconstructions: ‘Even within this select company … exceptional’; he quotes Le Roy Ladurie (New York Review of Books, 1983) calling it a ‘major work of historical reconstruction’ (p. 554; mediated). Holberg committee (2010): it ‘demonstrated to a broader public how an individual event in early modern France could illuminate overall mentalities’. The book is unread; the French edition (1982) appeared with the film.

proposed_edges.relationship: Finlay charges an ‘excess of invention’ against ‘the sovereignty of the sources’ in her Bertrande de Rols; Davis answers that where reconstruction stops and invention begins was ‘precisely the question’ the book posed (1988)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Robert Finlay’s intervention in the debate over evidence in microhistory (micro/reconstruction_invention), not a verdict of the field. Finlay, AHR 93:3 (1988), 553–571, read in full: ‘Davis fails to show that her view of women in peasant society is relevant to the case she is examining’ (p. 557); ‘self-fashioning’ ‘is merely imposed on the historical record as an ingenious assertion’ (p. 564); ‘If historical records can be bypassed so thoroughly in the service of an inventive blend of intuition and assertion, it is difficult to see what distinguishes the writing of history from that of fiction’ (p. 569); ‘speculation, whether founded on intuition or on concepts drawn from anthropology and literary criticism, is supposed to give way before the sovereignty of the sources … Davis has permitted an excess of invention’ (p. 571). He praises ‘its eloquent portrait of peasant life … its emphasis on the central role of women’ (p. 569). Davis, ‘On the Lame’, AHR 93:3 (1988), 572–603, read in part: the question ‘is precisely the question I hoped readers would ask and reflect on’; she would have preferred a critique ‘more subject to “the sovereignty of sources” to which it claims loyalty’ (p. 572); ‘he plays Savonarola to my Montaigne. Fortunately, historical practice can profit from each stance’ (p. 574); ‘proto-feminist’ is ‘a careless reporting of my text’ (p. 584). The group endpoint locates Finlay’s critique within the debate over microhistorical reconstruction; it does not assign him membership in a school. Ginzburg’s 1984 postface to the Italian edition, cited by Finlay (p. 569 n. 71), is unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: A narrative of four charivaris cited by Stone among works turning to narrative, after she criticised his draft (1979); later, pardon tales read as crafted stories without discrediting the archives (1987)
proposed_edges.map_label: Charivari narrative; Fiction in the Archives, 1979–87
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Stone, Past & Present 85 (1979), read: p. 3, starred note, thanks ‘Natalie Davis’ among colleagues ‘for valuable criticism of an early draft of this paper’; p. 18: ‘Natalie Davis has presented a narrative of four charivaris or ritual public shame procedures in seventeenth-century Lyon and Geneva, in order to illustrate community efforts to enforce public standards of honour and propriety’ (n. 29, the essay forthcoming in Le Goff and Schmitt, Le charivari). Her own account (1997, p. 21, read): she called her 1987 book Fiction in the Archives ‘somewhat to the consternation of Lawrence Stone to whom it was dedicated’; ‘“fiction” referred not to falsification, but to the crafting element in everything we do and say. Rather than being on an extreme anti-foundationalist mission to discredit the archives, I was presenting them as a source of new evidence’. As the revival scope requires, being named by Stone does not imply that she accepted his diagnosis. Fiction in the Archives is unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Bloch’s Strange Defeat and Feudal Society as formative reading in her turn from the history of ideas to social history; Bloch and Power as the twentieth-century historians of her AHA address (1940s–1987)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own retrospect (1997, read in full): ‘Before I graduated, I also read Marc Bloch’s Strange Defeat and learned that an historian can be a hero’ (p. 5); ‘I had been reading Marc Bloch’s Feudal Society, and was all ready when W. K. Jordan urged me take Ket’s Rebellion’ as her graduate work shifted ‘from the history of ideas to social history’ (p. 7); arriving in Lyon in 1952, ‘I rushed around Lyon … to find a monument to Marc Bloch’ (p. 8). Her AHA presidential address (1987; read in part through tool excerpts) considers ‘history’s two bodies’ through five historians, Bloch and Eileen Power among them, and per the tool’s summary ends on Bloch’s 1942 letter. An acknowledged formative reading recorded in retrospect; it does not make her an Annales historian: she wrote that its histoire totale ‘could not serve as a model for what I wanted to do’ (p. 13).

proposed_edges.relationship: Decentred comparison: European women’s lives set beside colonial domination and non-European respondents (1995), a Muslim traveller between worlds (2006), and a programme of ‘decentering history’ (2010)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own retrospect (1997, read): Women on the Margins was to ‘expand the single microhistory into a decentered comparison of three European lives’ (p. 21); she asked about ‘the uninvited French intrusion into the American woodlands’ and Merian’s ‘African and Indian slaves’ (p. 22), introduced ‘non-European women … not just as silent objects … but as active respondents’ (p. 22), and felt ‘permanently relocated as an historian of Europe’, with a new project on ‘cultural mixture’ along ‘the caravan routes of North Africa’ (p. 23). The conclusion of Women on the Margins (davis_margins_primary, earlier reading) shows marginality coexisting with colonial domination. Holberg committee (2010, read): ‘connecting early modern Europe with new areas of comparative history, exploring cultural, geographical and religious interchange’; Women on the Margins and Trickster Travels explore ‘the translation and transmission of cultures’. ‘Decentering History’ (Holberg Symposium, 2010; abstract only) moves ‘beyond a focus on Europe or the West’. Hesse (2024): ‘there were no dark parts of the globe’. Trickster Travels (2006) and the 2011 article are unread. Subrahmanyam’s mediated link from Kafadar to Davis (1997) stays on edge_641.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: No carlo_ginzburg node. Her citation of Ginzburg’s ‘Clues’ (On the Lame, n. 11) is recorded on nzd_rel_08; Ginzburg’s ‘Prove e possibilità’ (1984 postface) is unread.
Desan’s 1989 chapter is unread; Hunt’s one-line characterisation is too mediated for a critique edge.

She names Geertz among anthropologists read eclectically and records co-teaching; no specific use is established. Folded into nzd_rel_07; edges 005/040 notes updated.

Only her retrospect (1997, p. 10) and Nussdorfer’s memorial; ‘Printing and the People’ is unread.

verification.note: Read for revision 1.143 (data/extension-2026/davis-backfill-2026-10-17/evidence-davis.md §1): read in full in the ACLS PDF text layer. Printed folios 10–23 appear in the text; folios 1–9 were fixed from the constant PDF offset (PDF page = printed page + 6), checked against 10–23. The unsigned ACLS preface is unpaginated and is a separate reader statement. Passages used: Bloch, Strange Defeat (p. 5) and Feudal Society (p. 7); Marx and Weber tested on Lyon (p. 7); history of the book (p. 10); multiple social axes (p. 11); ‘A Trade Union’ (1966) and Hobsbawm (pp. 12–13); Annales histoire totale ‘could not serve as a model’ (p. 13); Van Gennep, Bakhtin, and reading Evans-Pritchard, Turner, Geertz and Mintz ‘eclectically’ (p. 14); Society and Culture and ‘Rites’ (p. 15); the 1971 course with Jill Conway, ‘the first course in women’s history in Canada’ (p. 16); film and ‘anthropological history’ (pp. 17–18); ‘I came to microhistory (or what I called ethnography) via film’ and co-teaching with Geertz (p. 19); Fiction in the Archives and Stone (p. 21); ‘a decentered comparison of three European lives’ (p. 21); margins and colonial intrusion (p. 22); ‘permanently relocated as an historian of Europe’ (p. 23). Retrospective testimony (1997): evidence of how she later described her work, not of what the earlier works say.

verification.note: Read for revision 1.143 (data/extension-2026/davis-backfill-2026-10-17/evidence-davis.md §8): AHA web text read in part through the WebFetch tool (three passes), which returns only short exact quotations; the AHA site refuses plain HTTP clients. Quoted: the header (‘A paper read at the annual meeting of the American Historical Association, December 28, 1987’); ‘I want to consider how historians have conceptualized the body of historical knowledge’; ‘Eileen Power was one of the creators of a new kind of social and economic history in England’; the main text says ‘only one female historian contributed an essay to it [the Annales] in the seventeen years of its existence’, and note 65 then discusses Thérèse Sclafert (‘has an article in the first volume (1929) of the Annales’) and Lucie Varga (‘a refugee from Austria’, who ‘contributed an ethnographic study of an Austrian valley’), calling Varga ‘the only other woman writing for the Annales’. The main text’s count and the note’s two names are not reconciled here. The tool reported, without exact quotation, that the five historians are Pasquier, Hume, Catharine Macaulay, Marc Bloch and Eileen Power and that the conclusion quotes Bloch’s 1942 letter. No AHR page numbers. Crossref: doi:10.1086/ahr/93.1.1.

new_sources.title: Natalie Zemon Davis, “Decentering History: Local Stories and Cultural Crossings in a Global World,” lecture, Holberg Prize Symposium, Bergen, June 2010; published in History and Theory 50, no. 2 (2011): 188–202.
new_sources.citation: Natalie Zemon Davis, “Decentering History: Local Stories and Cultural Crossings in a Global World,” lecture, Holberg Prize Symposium, Bergen, June 2010; published in History and Theory 50, no. 2 (2011): 188–202.

verification.note: Abstract only, read for revision 1.143 on a lecture-video listing through the WebFetch tool (exact excerpts): the lecture ‘describes the expansion of historical writing in the decades after World War II’ ‘to include the study of working people and other non-elite populations and women’ ‘and to move beyond a focus on Europe or the West’, with ‘a comparison of the literary careers of Ibn Khaldun and Christine de Pizan’ and ‘the transmission and transformation of practices of divination, healing, and detection from Africa’ ‘to the slave communities of Suriname’. The 2011 journal citation is from a search-indexed footnote, not opened; the article is unread (an IAS repository copy returned 403). Delivery the day before the 9 June 2010 ceremony is per the Holberg memorial (nzd_holberg_2010).

new_sources.title: Judith Jackson Fossett, “Slaves You Have Never Seen,” review of Natalie Zemon Davis, Slaves on Screen, Common-place 1, no. 4 (July 2001).
new_sources.citation: Judith Jackson Fossett, “Slaves You Have Never Seen,” review of Natalie Zemon Davis, Slaves on Screen, Common-place 1, no. 4 (July 2001).

verification.note: Read for revision 1.143 through the WebFetch tool (exact short excerpts). Fossett reports Davis’s question ‘How can film best be used as a medium for presenting history?’ and her claim that ‘we can take film seriously as a source of valuable and even innovative historical vision’; she criticises ‘perhaps a misleading title’, says the volume ‘would have benefited from even a cursory consideration’ of post-Civil Rights black filmmakers and writers, that it ‘raises more questions than it answers’ and that its final question ‘remains largely unanswered’.

new_sources.title: Holberg Prize Committee, recommendation for awarding the 2010 Holberg Prize to Natalie Zemon Davis, reproduced in “In Memoriam: 2010 Holberg Laureate Natalie Zemon Davis,” holbergprize.org (31 October 2023).
new_sources.citation: Holberg Prize Committee, recommendation for awarding the 2010 Holberg Prize to Natalie Zemon Davis, reproduced in “In Memoriam: 2010 Holberg Laureate Natalie Zemon Davis,” holbergprize.org (31 October 2023).

verification.note: Read for revision 1.143 (data/extension-2026/davis-backfill-2026-10-17/evidence-davis.md §9): read in full (HTML). The committee’s 2010 text, reproduced ‘in extenso’, is distinguished from the 2023 memorial wording. Quoted: ‘not hostage to any particular school of thought or politics’; ‘Her work brings gender to the fore’; ‘The uniqueness of her work lies in connecting early modern Europe with new areas of comparative history, exploring cultural, geographical and religious interchange’; Society and Culture ‘widely acknowledged as path-breaking’; Martin Guerre ‘demonstrated to a broader public how an individual event in early modern France could illuminate overall mentalities’; The Gift ‘has been called a model of historical anthropology’; Women on the Margins and Trickster Travels explore ‘the translation and transmission of cultures’; ‘inspired many younger historians’. The memorial records the ‘Decentering History’ lecture at the symposium before the 9 June 2010 ceremony.

new_sources.citation: Carla A. Hesse, “Natalie Zemon Davis (1928–2023),” Perspectives on History (American Historical Association), 4 March 2024.

verification.note: Read for revision 1.143 through the WebFetch tool (exact excerpts only; the site refuses plain HTTP clients). Quoted: ‘Natalie Zemon Davis was the most renowned anglophone historian of early modern France of her generation’; her corpus ‘had a transformative impact in academia and beyond’; ‘She was methodologically heterodox, incorporating anthropological and literary approaches’; ‘Her most transformative course was Society and the Sexes, a first in introducing the history of women’ [into university curricula]; ‘In her historical imagination, there were no dark parts of the globe’. Hesse quotes an unpublished letter in which Thompson, ‘her friend’, wrote that she ‘used the theories and methods she needed’ (mediated).

scott_gender_1986.note: Revision 1.143: printed p. 1054 read (OCR of the same scan). Those who wanted ‘a relational notion’ used ‘gender’; ‘Thus Natalie Davis suggested in 1975, “It seems to me that we should be interested in the history of both women and men … Our goal is to understand the significance of the sexes, of gender groups in the historical past …”’ (n. 4: Feminist Studies 3, Winter 1975–76, p. 90). Davis’s words are as Scott quotes them.

davis_scs_memorial.note: Revision 1.143: read in full; the memorial is by Laurie Nussdorfer (Wesleyan University). Passages: she ‘became the rare social historian who valued printed sources’, asking who produced them and ‘what constituted their stake in the radical new technology of print’; on Martin Guerre, ‘Natalie was dissatisfied with a mere drama; she had a deeper historian’s question’; plenary at the society’s first conference (1969); two SCS prizes in her honour (2023) in early modern women’s, gender and sexuality studies.

new_people.label: Robert Finlay
new_people.identity_note: Robert Finlay, historian of Renaissance Venice, whose book on Venetian government Davis cites (On the Lame, 1988); critic of The Return of Martin Guerre in the AHR Forum (1988). Added in revision 1.143. Not grounded in Wikidata: two Wikidata MCP searches on 2026-10-17 found no matching item.

row.context: Scott (1986) quotes her 1975–76 call to study ‘the history of both women and men’ and ‘the significance of the sexes, of gender groups’ as an early relational use of gender. A precursor statement, not a founding of the field.
row.works: “‘Women’s History’ in Transition: The European Case” (1976), as quoted by Scott (1986)

row.context: What she later called a ‘decentered comparison’ of three European women’s lives, keeping colonial domination and non-European respondents in view (1995; her 1997 retrospect); Trickster Travels (2006), which the Holberg committee groups with it as exploring ‘the translation and transmission of cultures’; and a programme of ‘decentering history’ (2010; abstract read).
row.works: Women on the Margins (1995); Trickster Travels (2006); “Decentering History” (Holberg Symposium lecture, 2010)

row.context: Read Goubert and Le Roy Ladurie with her students but found that Annales histoire totale ‘could not serve as a model’ for her urban, religious and women’s history (1997). Her presidential address examines women’s limited place in the early Annales; note 65 discusses Thérèse Sclafert and Lucie Varga.
row.works: A Life of Learning (1997), p. 13; “History’s Two Bodies” (AHA presidential address, 1987)

row.context: Charges an ‘excess of invention’ in Davis’s portrait of Bertrande de Rols and insists on ‘the sovereignty of the sources’, while praising her portrait of peasant life; Davis replied in the same AHR Forum.

Historical consultant to the film Le Retour de Martin Guerre (1982), wanting the book to reach audiences ‘from the villagers of Artigat whom I had interviewed’ to specialists; Slaves on Screen (2000) takes film ‘seriously as a source of valuable and even innovative historical vision’ (as Fossett quotes her), and Fossett finds that it ‘raises more questions than it answers’. The atlas has no separate history-and-film entry.
row.works: Le Retour de Martin Guerre (film, 1982); Slaves on Screen (2000)
